body: There’s fog this morning, the first in a week and by the look of it the last: a thin marine layer laid against the window of 412 like breath on a cold mirror, already coming apart over the Grove, where the tops of the eucalyptus stand up out of it one at a time. By nine it will be blue again.

On the desk, squared under the Augustine, is his friendship paper with her red in it. Page one he could recite: *No.* *Cite me.* *This is Aristotle wearing your jacket.* Page two he hasn’t turned to since Sunday night. He knows where *Defense.* is on it anyway.

Monday at one, in Hollis 302, she said, “Good afternoon, Jack.” Pleasant, pressed, and addressed to nobody in particular, like the card that comes with flowers. Five weeks at that table and she had never once called him Jack across it. “Afternoon, Lena.” Caleb looked from one of them to the other, then up at the whiteboard, as if the rules might be posted. Then Hale gave them the week. Lying: Augustine, *De mendacio*; Kant and the murderer at the door; Aquinas, the Second Part of the Second Part, question one hundred and ten. And the papers, due Wednesday. Mr. Costigan: “That a Lie Can Be a Kindness.” Miss Broussard: “That Every Lie Is a Sin.” Each of them the side they least believed they could prove. Hale looked from one to the other, delighted, as though somebody had left a present on his end of the table. Nobody has said a word about any of it. It’s just how things are now.

Michaelmas: Michael, Gabriel and Raphael, and Michael first. The medal is on its chain beside the Augustine, where he took it off to shower. Nonna’s rule, older than he is: on your saint’s day he goes on the outside of the shirt, *così vede*, so he can see out. Jack puts it on over the flannel and lets it hang.

Under the Frette, Theo’s iPhone is already lit. One green eye comes up over the edge of the sheet. “Who’s he?” “St. Michael.” The thumb goes on moving on the screen. “He throws the devil out of heaven.” “Does he catch anybody?” Theo says, scrolling. “Or just throw?”
Jack has nothing for that, and by the time he’s looked, Theo is somewhere else on the phone entirely. Then he turns it around and holds it up.

body: Michaelmas at the 12:10: white on the altar and white on Osei, and a gold thread in the stole that catches whenever he turns. Twenty-odd people under the long upturned hull of the ceiling, and the noon coming down through the blue glass in long cool bars across the pews. Kevin, in a navy quarter-zip, has saved Jack a seat with a Bible open to the day. Two rows up is Becca Lindell, between labs, her rosary wound twice around her wrist.
Lena is across the aisle in Mrs. Fitch’s pew by the shrine, at Mrs. Fitch’s elbow. Last Tuesday she came in late and slid in beside Jack without a word. Today she came early.

The lector, a graduate student with a cold, gets through the dragon in Revelation with only one sniff. *Michael and his angels battled against the dragon.* Osei reads the Gospel himself: Philip bringing Nathanael, and Nathanael, under his fig tree, unconvinced about Nazareth. *Here is a true Israelite. There is no duplicity in him.*

Osei preaches from the step, and briefly. “The old translations say *guile*. I prefer it. Guile sounds like something a man could put down, if he wanted to.” He considers them, the old man with the cane and the nursing girls and Kevin. “And notice that Our Lord says it of only one man, and the man was sitting under a tree minding his own business.” He sits.

After the dismissal nobody moves, because it’s the feast and Osei isn’t finished. “Saint Michael the Archangel,” he begins, and the old people come in on *defend us in battle* without needing a card. Jack says it with them, the medal out on his shirt. From the pew by the shrine, under Mrs. Fitch’s quaver, so does Lena.

In the vestibule Mrs. Fitch has Lena by the holy water and is telling her about roses. Thursday she’ll bring the first of the Peace roses off her own bush, for the Little Flower, “every year since 1979, and not one year they didn’t open.” Lena listens with her whole face, and Mrs. Fitch blooms under it. “She’s my middle name,” Lena says.

Mrs. Fitch is delighted. She puts a hand on her own heart and then on Lena’s arm, and promises her a rose of her own on Thursday, to take home in a cup. Jack is right behind them with his fingers still wet from the font, and he hears it.
Lena turns. Her eyes go first to the medal on the outside of his shirt. “Happy feast day, Jack.” “Thank you.” Then, pleasantly, as if he’d asked: “Ten days till Columbus Day weekend.”

Becca catches up with them at the door, backpack on one shoulder, and points at him the second she sees him. “Don’t ask! Saturday. Don’t *ask*.” Then, past him, beaming: “Hi, Lena!” “Becca,” Lena says, “that’s lovely, whatever it is.” Becca laughs and is off across the courtyard toward the Marine Lab at a ranch walk, late for something with a microscope in it.

response: “We’re fine, Jack.”
She says it kindly. Then she takes Mrs. Fitch’s arm, and the two of them go down the steps into the sun, talking about aphids.
*Fine.*
At two he’s on La Flaca, freewheeling down Mission Street toward Driftwood Books for no reason he would give out loud.

She startles. “How did you — ” “You just told Mrs. Fitch.” “So I did.” Something crosses her face that is very nearly her real smile, and she folds it away before it’s finished, and goes down the steps with Mrs. Fitch.
At two he’s chaining La Flaca to the meter outside Driftwood Books, and he knows exactly what he’s looking for.
Lena laughs, politely: the laugh she gives Caleb when Caleb says *Selah*. It’s worse than none. She goes down the steps with Mrs. Fitch.
By two he’s on La Flaca, headed down Mission toward Driftwood Books with the medal bouncing on his shirt.
He lets her. She goes down the steps into the sun with Mrs. Fitch’s arm through hers, bending her head to hear about aphids. Kevin, at Jack’s shoulder, has the decency to look at the olive tree.
At two he’s on La Flaca, headed down Mission toward Driftwood Books.

body: At two he chained La Flaca to the meter outside Driftwood Books, Ray’s light still clipped to the handlebar, and went through the cart out front the way he always does, spine by spine. Boethius was asleep on the register. Mrs. Danvers watched him from the top of the poetry shelf, unimpressed. Thérèse of Lisieux, *Story of a Soul*: the ICS edition, John Clarke’s translation, three dollars in pencil inside the cover, and somebody’s yellow highlighter through the first part, every other sentence, until about page sixty, where it gives up, as if the owner lost faith or a pen. It’s in his back pocket now. The Augustine stayed on the desk. He bought it an hour after she told Mrs. Fitch, and he hasn’t asked himself why, and isn’t going to.

At five, the mailboxes. Marcus at the front desk under his orgo. In Jack’s box, one envelope, the corner in block capitals: TRUMBULL CORRECTIONAL INSTITUTION, and the number. He doesn’t open it in the lobby. He takes the east stairs to the landing where the window opens its six inches, and sits on the top step with the Lagoon going gold, and opens it there.

body: Hollis 302 at two minutes to one, and Hale is already in his chair. For five weeks the rest of them have been seated before the door ever opened for him; today the roster is squared on the oak in front of him and his hands are folded on top of it, and Caleb, coming in with his *Consolations* shedding Post-its, checks his watch and then the wall clock to see which of them is wrong.

At one exactly: “St. Jerome,” Hale says. “Translated the whole of the Bible, insulted everyone he ever met, with one exception — a Roman widow named Paula. Rome ran him out of town over her. She followed him to Bethlehem, and they buried him beside her. Rome later stole the body back, which is very Rome.” His eye travels down the table and stops. “Mr. Costigan’s thesis, in a hair shirt.”
The table laughs. Lena uncaps her pen.
The papers cross at the top of the hour the way they always do. Hers comes to him squared to the edge of the table; his goes to her the same way. “Thanks.” “Thanks.”

Then the texts. Augustine, *De mendacio*: no lie, ever, not even to save a life. Kant, 1797: the murderer at the door asks whether your friend is in the house, and you may not lie to him. And Thomas, the Second Part of the Second Part, question one hundred and ten: every lie a sin; the helpful lie, the one told to spare somebody, only venial; and the Hebrew midwives in Exodus, who lied to Pharaoh to save the boys and were rewarded for it — not for the lie, says Thomas, but for their fear of God and their mercy.

What follows is forty minutes. Lena makes a point and Jack concedes it before she’s finished making it. Jack makes one and Lena says, “That’s right,” and builds a small neat porch on the front of it. She gives him the joking lie without a fight; he gives her the murderer, the door, the friend in the cellar. Yusuf draws load arrows in his margin with less and less conviction. Hale watches it the way he’d watch a cricket match in which both sides have agreed to bowl underarm, and at twenty past he says, “Somebody fetch a priest. The Catholics are agreeing.”
At half past one: “Mr. Costigan, last week you argued both sides of a question and won twice. Today you’ve argued neither and are losing to the radiator.” The radiator, on cue, knocks.
“I forgive you, by the way,” Lena says to the table, turning a page. “For last week.”

Yusuf puts his pen down. “There’s a hadith,” he says. “Umm Kulthum, in Sahih Muslim. The Prophet allowed it in three cases. In war. To make peace between people. And what a husband says to his wife, and a wife to her husband.” He looks round the table. “The third one’s load-bearing.” “Marriage is a war,” Caleb says. “Then you’re covered twice.”
“All very tidy,” Hale says. “The commonest lie in the world is not told to murderers at doors. It’s told to policemen, about the dead, by people who loved them.”
Lena’s hand goes to the medal. Hale looks at the window. Jack’s pen has stopped in the middle of a word.

Then Hale has his voice back, all the Oxford on it. “Two pages for Monday. Lie to me convincingly.” And down the table, to the two of them, very nearly pleading: “I’d settle for one real disagreement. Anyone?”

journal.title: Designated antagonists
journal.text: Two pages a week, bled on in red. Week two, hers: “That a Broken Statue Is Still Herakles,” with my sentence on page two. Mine: “That God Is the One Who Pays.” She kept it. Then Hale said it out loud: prove the thing you least believe you can prove. Moral luck — mine: “That the Lucky Man Owes Nothing.” Hers: “That There Is Such a Thing as Luck.” Her red on mine: “You don’t believe a word of this. It’s your best paper.” Friendship. Mine: “That a Man and a Woman Can Be Friends.” Hers: “That They Can’t.” She kept mine, and sent it back with *Defense.* in the margin. This week, lying. Mine: “That a Lie Can Be a Kindness.” Hers: “That Every Lie Is a Sin.” We agreed with each other for an hour. Hale asked for a priest.

response: “Thomas rewards the mercy and not the lie,” Jack says. “But it wasn’t two things. Shiphrah looked Pharaoh in the face and told him the Hebrew women deliver before the midwife gets there. That sentence *was* the mercy. You can’t damn one and crown the other. ‘Every lie’ can’t carry the midwives without help.” Lena, at once, pleasantly: “That’s fair.” Hale puts his face in his hands. “She *agreed* with you. Christ.”
At half past two the chairs scrape, and Lena is gone before he’s got his bag shut.
“Lent is a lie told to the stomach, Mr. Costigan,” Hale says, “and the stomach always knows.” A laugh goes round the table. Lena is already turning a page.
At half past two the chairs scrape, and Lena is gone before he’s got his bag shut.

choices.text: “The midwives are the hardest case in the book. I can’t answer them.”
response: Lena looks up from her notes at that. Then back down. Hale regards Jack with real sorrow. “Honesty,” he says. “How dreary. Monday.”
At half past two the chairs scrape, and Lena is gone before he’s got his bag shut.

He lets the clock have it. Yusuf and Caleb take the last ten minutes, on whether a man praying in tongues he doesn’t understand can be lying (Caleb, with feeling: yes). Hale stands. “Go. All of you. Jerome would’ve had you flogged.”
The chairs scrape, and Lena is gone before he’s got his bag shut.

s13.slug: SATURDAY · 12:52 PM · DELGADO HALL, EAST STAIRWELL, 4TH-FLOOR LANDING
body: Eight minutes to one on the landing, eight minutes to four on Glenwood Avenue, and the whole east stairwell smells of sun on concrete. Jack’s shirt still has the courtyard in it, dust and olive leaf and a little dog. His mother answers on the second ring and starts with his father.

The union hall Tuesday, she says. There’s a list. “Your father’s on it.” A recall list, for when, nobody said. They’re talking about the small car for Lordstown, the Cruze. “Next year, maybe.” And then the number on the news Friday, nine-point-eight, which she says twice. “Highest since 1983, Jackie.”
A click: the extension in the front room. “Indiana tonight,” his father says. “I’ll find it.” “Ma says the Cruze — ” “We’ll see,” his father says. Click.

Rosie wants a crab for her birthday, his mother says. Wednesday, eight years old, and what she wants is a crab. A live one. “I told her we live in Ohio.” “There’s one in the mail,” Jack says. “A *crab*?” “A drawing of one.” “Thank God.”

Then a scuffle on the line, and the bedroom extension, and EWTN low behind it. “Giacomino.” Nonna doesn’t say hello on the telephone; she considers it implied. “E la ragazza?” “Ma, I told you,” his mother says from the kitchen phone. “She has a *fidanzato*.” Glenwood Avenue is quiet for a second. “Peccato,” Nonna says. Pity. And then, sharp as the paring knife she still won’t let anybody else use: “E l’altra?”
*And the other one?*

body.text: “Ha mangiato?” Nonna says, not waiting. “Le è piaciuto?” Did she eat. Did she like it. He tells her yes, every bite, and she asked for the recipe for her mother, and she’d never heard of the breadcrumbs, *la mollica*, Nonna, never in her life — and Nonna is pleased, and tells him again about the anchovies, how they have to melt, and his mother gets a word in about the Iannuccis’ dog. Then, five minutes on, out of nowhere, new: “Giacomino. Ha mangiato? Le è piaciuto?” His mother takes the phone back.
body.else: Jack laughs, and has no answer for her in either language, and Nonna has already handed the phone back to his mother, satisfied, as if she’d won something.

body: His mother, after a while, carefully, as if it were only a question: “Is Idaho going home for Thanksgiving?” He says he doesn’t know. She lets that be the end of it, for now, and tells him to eat.

journal.title: Nonna
journal.text: Asked me about the girl. Laughed. Five minutes later she asked me again, the same words, like it was the first time. Ma says she’s tired. It’s the nineteenth. Michaelmas she lit one for me and one for Danny. Saturday: ‘E la ragazza?’ Ma told her about Wes. ‘Peccato.’ Then, sharp: ‘E l’altra?’

response: At twenty past three he walks over in the heat: the Grove smelling like cough drops in the sun, Ocean Road shimmering, the courtyard gate warm under his hand.
He lies down at one with the window open and is gone at once, four hours flat and dreamless, like his father between doubles at Lordstown.

s13b.slug: SATURDAY · 3:31 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE CONFESSIONAL
body: The courtyard at half past three is all glare and no people. The olive tree throws one small coin of shade. A dog’s water bowl has been forgotten by the door, and the sprinkler’s brass head points at nothing. As Jack comes in at the gate, somebody is going out at the far side, toward Ocean Road: Lena, in the oatmeal cardigan in the heat, her face scrubbed and very still. She doesn’t see him. He eases the gate shut so it won’t clack.

On the coat-closet door the card still says KNOCK (gently). He knocks gently. “Come.” Lemon polish over old wool. The kneeler with its cracked maroon vinyl, the chair beside it so you can choose, the linen screen with the lamp behind it so that Osei is a shape. Jack kneels.
“Bless me, Father, for I have sinned.” He says how long. Then he says it, all of it that’s his. A night on the beach, the whole night, and how glad he was of it.

body: When he’s finished, the shape behind the linen is quiet a while. Then Osei says, in the voice he uses for everyone who has ever knelt there: “Be truthful with the one you’re with. Truthful is not the same as cruel.” The lamp hums. “A good man can do a great deal of harm being careful.” For a penance, a decade, “and something small and true, for the one who is praying for you. You will know what. Small is important.”

Jack says the Act of Contrition. On the linen the shadow of a hand lifts. “…through the ministry of the Church may God give you pardon and peace, and I absolve you from your sins in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” “Amen.”

Outside, the glare again, and the forgotten bowl. He sits on the low wall in the olive tree’s one coin of shade and says the decade there, slowly, counting on his fingers. Then he gets on La Flaca and goes to work.

body.text: He came in at seven with the light still on the harbor and the afternoon still on him, and it has held up surprisingly well through four hours of the Hobart.

body: By twenty to midnight the Saturday rush has gone home and left its plates. Two fishermen at the counter are arguing about a winch. Somebody’s quarter has Bobby Darin going on the jukebox, and the board over the register says PIE OF THE DAY: CHERRY.

Gloria comes down the line with the coffee pot and stops at the pass, the pencil through her gray bun, and looks at him through the steam off the Hobart. “You’ve got the face of a man with a secret and a stomachache,” she says. “Which is it?” “Both.” “Start with the secret.”
So he tells her about Friday.

body.text: The Newman kitchen. Nonna’s Friday sauce, the anchovies melted down to nothing, the breadcrumbs instead of cheese. Mrs. Fitch in the doorway with a crossword, chaperoning.
The elephant seals at Piedras Blancas at sunset, a beach full of them, in Kevin’s van, and fish after in Cambria.
Two horses on the dunes at sunset. Hers did what she told it. His did what it liked.

body: And the girl. Idaho: a ranch, seven brothers and sisters. She has pulled a calf, she says grace like she’s signing a contract, and this morning she brought a hermit crab to the Blessing of the Animals in a Tupperware and named it after the First Way. He asked, he tells Gloria. He paid.
Gloria shuts her eyes, the pot still in her hand, and rates her sight unseen. “Apple,” she says. She opens them. “Hon, that’s the one you bring home to your mother.”

At the flattop Rudy doesn’t turn around. He scrapes the grill once, end to end. “It knew, didn’t it.” “It knew.”

body: Gloria moves down to wipe the counter in front of the fishermen, who have settled the winch, and she doesn’t look up from the rag. “What happened to the pecan?”

journal.title: The Anchor
journal.text: Marionberry: 4/10. Olallieberry: 9/10 — Dad would eat two pieces and complain about the second. Gloria rated Lena: pecan. She rated Margot without meeting her: rhubarb — tart, and nobody can decide if it’s a fruit. She rated Becca without meeting her: apple. The one you bring home to your mother. Then she asked what happened to the pecan. A whole pie for a funeral is half price. I work here Tue/Thu/Sat, seven to one. Once a year the kitchen goes dark on a Thursday.

response: “Hm,” Gloria says. She goes on wiping the same clean place on the Formica for a while. Then she takes the pot down the counter to the fishermen.
Gloria stops wiping. “That’s what I was afraid of, hon.” She pours him a cup of coffee he didn’t ask for, sets it on the pass by the Hobart, and goes.
“Pecan’s not seasonal, hon,” Gloria says. “Pecan’s forever.” She folds the rag in half, and in half again. “That’s the trouble with pecan.”
She gives him a look over the coffee pot with thirty years of this counter in it. “Sure it is,” she says.
